references.text: The Lord calls the steward to account. The theme of giving an account of one's stewardship is also found in [ref:Luk 12:42-46|Luke 12:42-46], where Jesus speaks about the faithful and wise steward whom the Lord puts in charge of his household, and what happens if he fails in his responsibility.

In the parable of the minas in [ref:Luk 19:12-26|Luke 19:12-26], the nobleman demands an account from his servants for what he has entrusted to them – the same principle of being accountable for entrusted goods.

In [ref:Matt 25:19-30|Matthew 25:19-30], the master returns and settles accounts with his servants in the parable of the talents, just as the steward in Luke 16 is also called to give an account of his stewardship.

[ref:Matt 18:23-34|Matthew 18:23-34] tells of a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants. The expression "ἀπόδος τὸν λόγον" (give an account) reflects the same requirement to be accountable.
Paul writes in [ref:Rom 14:12|Romans 14:12] that each of us will give an account of ourselves to God, confirming the biblical principle that we are all accountable for our stewardship.
In [ref:1 Pet 4:5|1 Peter 4:5], it is said that they will give an account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead – the same motif of giving an account as in the steward's situation.

[ref:Hebr 13:17|Hebrews 13:17] speaks of leaders who watch over souls and must give an account, emphasizing the same responsibility for entrusted stewardship that the steward in the parable is confronted with.

In [ref:Jes 22:15-19|Isaiah 22:15-19], Shebna is removed from his position as steward over the king's house because he has abused his office – an Old Testament parallel to the steward who loses his position due to poor stewardship.
